subject: Interaction between latent variable and observed variable

messages.author: ee65f9feb643484e
messages.subject: Interaction between latent variable and observed variable
parts:
I'm wondering how to include an interaction between a latent variable and a continuous observed variable in a model.

Suppose the latent variable is F, with indicators X1, X2, X3, and suppose the other observed variable is X4. Would it make sense to have the product X4.F as a latent variable with indicators X4.X1, X4.X2 and X4.X3? Or is there a better way?

Thanks,
Mark

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Interaction between latent variable and observed variable
parts:
Mark--
What is the distribution of the observed variable like?  If it discrete with large n, you might consider using its values to define multiple groups, and evaluating the interaction in terms of differences in parameter estimates across groups.  If the observed variable is discrete but with few observations for some values, maybe you collapse some smaller categories.  But if the distribution is continuous, then yes, the product indicator approach makes total sense.  If it seems strange, think of giving the single indicator its own factor, and then you are back in the factor X factor interaction scenario.
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

messages.subject: RE: Interaction between latent variable and observed variable
parts:
Mark—

     The factor model for F2 will not be identified if you allow free covariance among residuals for all of F2’s indicators, as this code does.  F2 needs to be the avenue for shared variance—with all residual covariances free, there is no need for F2.  Lavaan does not strongly indicate that an identification problem exists.  Comment out the free residual covariances—you did not assign them any values when setting up the simulation.

--Ed Rigdon

On 12/19/2014 04:40 AM, Mark Seeto wrote:
> Thank you for your reply, Ed. I assume you meant free covariance among
> residuals of F1.x4's indicators.
>
> When I remove those free covariances, the F2 ~ F1 estimate is about the
> same as before (1.3, compared to the true value of 0.7):

But that is to be expected. It has nothing to do with the product
indicator approach. This is due to the interaction effect. If we
simplify this to a linear model, you can see what is going on:

set.seed(1)
n <- 10000 # sample size
rho <- 0 # correlation between F1 and x4
var.F1 <- 2 # variance of F1
var.x4 <- 3 # variance of x4
cov.F1x4 <- rho*sqrt(var.F1*var.x4) # covariance between F1 and x4
mean.x4 <- 2 # mean of x4
# First column of D is F1, second column is x4
D <- rmvnorm(n, mean = c(0, mean.x4), sigma = matrix(c(var.F1, cov.F1x4,
cov.F1x4, var.x4), nrow=2))

beta1 <- 0.7 # F2 ~ F1 coefficient
beta2 <- 0.5 # F2 ~ x4 coefficient
beta3 <- 0.3 # F2 ~ F1.x4 coefficient

var.resF2 <- 0.2 # F2 residual variance

F2 <- beta1*D[, 1] + beta2*D[, 2] + beta3*D[, 1]*D[, 2] + rnorm(n, 0,
sqrt(var.resF2))

F1 <- D[,1]

lm(F2 ~ F1)

parts:
Hi

I think that this this has to do with centering. The interaction means that slope of one variable (F1) depends on another variable (x4). To get the direct effect of F1, you must choose were from the regression plane to take it. If you center your data, then the effect of F1 is taken from the center of the regression plane so to speak and if not, it might be taken from the side. In your example x4 is not centered.


I use the  following R code to demonstrate this in class. Run it and compare the green line in the plot is centered and the blue line is not.

library(rgl)

x1 <- rnorm(100)+2
x2 <- rnorm(100)+2
y <- 0.2*x1 - 0.3*x2 +0.2*x1*x2  + rnorm(100, sd=0.3)

fit <- lm(y ~ x1*x2)
summary(fit)

plot3d(x1,x2,y, type="s", col="red", size=1)

coefs <- coef(fit)

resolution <- 20
x1c <- seq(from = min(x1), to = max(x1), length.out = resolution)
x2c <- seq(from = min(x2), to = max(x2), length.out = resolution)

surface3d(x1c, x2c, 
          predict(fit, data.frame(x1 = rep(x1c, resolution), x2 = rep(x1c, each = resolution))),
          front="lines",
          back="lines")

linecoords <- expand.grid(x1 = c(min(x1),max(x1)),
                          x2 = c(mean(x2),0))

linecoords$y <-  predict(fit,linecoords)

lines3d(linecoords[1:2,]$x1, linecoords[1:2,]$x2, linecoords[1:2,]$y, color="green", lwd = 20)
lines3d(linecoords[3:4,]$x1, linecoords[3:4,]$x2, linecoords[3:4,]$y, color="blue", lwd = 20)


Mikko

Aaron, here's an example that's a bit more general than the one above. I generated the data to be consistent with the "std.all" column.

library(lavaan)
library(mvtnorm)
library(semTools)

set.seed(1)

n <- 100000  # sample size

rho <- 0.6  # correlation between F1 and x4

var.F1 <- 1
var.x4 <- 1

cov.F1x4 <- rho*sqrt(var.F1*var.x4)  # covariance between F1 and x4; same as rho

mean.x4 <- 11

# First column of D is F1, second column is x4
D <- rmvnorm(n, mean = c(0, mean.x4),
             sigma = matrix(c(var.F1, cov.F1x4, cov.F1x4, var.x4), nrow=2))

beta1 <- 0.5  # F2 ~ F1
beta2 <- 0.4  # F2 ~ x4
beta3 <- 0.3  # F2 ~ F1.x4

# Residual variance of F2
var.resF2 <- 1 - (beta1^2 + beta2^2*var.x4 + beta3^2 + 2*beta1*beta2*cov.F1x4)  # 0.26
F2 <- beta1*D[, 1] + beta2*D[, 2] +

beta3*scale(D[, 1]*(D[, 2] - mean.x4)) + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var.resF2))
# Would be better to scale the product using the true mean and variance, but I don't know how to work
# out the true variance, so using the sample scaling will do.

# Indicator loadings
L1 <- 0.9
L2 <- 0.6
L3 <- 0.8
L5 <- 0.8
L6 <- 0.7
L7 <- 0.5

# Indicator residual variances
var1 <- 1 - L1^2  # 0.19
var2 <- 1 - L2^2  # 0.64
var3 <- 1 - L3^2  # 0.36
var5 <- 1 - L5^2  # 0.36
var6 <- 1 - L6^2  # 0.51
var7 <- 1 - L7^2  # 0.75

# Indicator intercepts
a1 <- 1
a2 <- 0
a3 <- 2
a5 <- 10
a6 <- 12
a7 <- 13

d0 <- data.frame(x1 = a1 + L1*D[, 1] + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var1)),
                 x2 = a2 + L2*D[, 1] + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var2)),
                 x3 = a3 + L3*D[, 1] + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var3)),
                 x4 = D[, 2],
                 x5 = a5 + L5*F2 + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var5)),
                 x6 = a6 + L6*F2 + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var6)),
                 x7 = a7 + L7*F2 + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var7)))

d <- indProd(d0, 1:3, 4, match=FALSE, meanC=TRUE, doubleMC=TRUE)

mod <- '

F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
F1.x4 =~ x1.x4 + x2.x4 + x3.x4
F2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7
F2 ~ F1 + x4 + F1.x4

messages.subject: Re: Interaction between latent variable and observed variable
parts:
Hi Sam,

Your question on model fit with a latent interaction model is a relevant one when using a product indicator approach. Product indicator approaches (double mean centering, residual centering), can bias model fit indices (e.g. RMSEA, CFI). Geldhof and colleagues (2013) discuss this issue with residual centering but the issue should also hold in double mean centering applications (short version, in these models the degrees of freedom are incorrect and need to be  corrected). An option in this situation is to  assess fit based on a "main effects" model without the interaction latent variable, acknowledging that this is a lower bound  for model fit for the model with the  interaction latent variable.

Alex

Geldhof, G. J., Pornprasertmanit, S., Schoemann, A. M., & Little, T. D. (2013). Orthogonalizing through residual centering extended applications and caveats. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 73(1), 27-46.
Chicago
